text: From this there follows another praise, which Johnson gives with his accustomed directness: "Shakespeare has no heroes; his scenes are occupied only by men" (Johnson 1765). He means that Shakespeare refused a practice common, in his judgement, with other dramatists, who lifted their persons above the level of mankind, furnished them with sentiments such as no living man would utter, and gave them a diction contrived rather to exact admiration than to produce belief. This refusal Johnson reckons among Shakespeare's principal merits. His persons speak as the reader might have spoken, had the same situation enclosed him and the same pressure been laid upon his mind; their words come out of ordinary life, and they affect us because in them we recognise our own nature. The rule is not suspended when the incident is beyond probability. A ghost upon the platform, or witches on the heath, belongs to a world outside familiar experience; but the men who hear and answer them remain within it. The marvel is in the action; the dialogue keeps the level of life. Hamlet questions his father's spirit as any son might question so dreadful an appearance, and Macbeth broods over the prophecy as an ambitious man would brood over the promise of a crown.
